paras: The lynching of Charles Mormon was the hanging of a Leadville stage driver by vigilantes at Durango, Colorado, in April 1881, after he was accused of shooting and killing Polk Prindle in a theater and gambling house. Vigilantes took him from the jail late at night and hanged him to a tree before a crowd of citizens, warning that anyone who cut him down before morning would be killed. A Denver Republican dispatch from Durango carried the story to papers across the country within days, and reprints spelled his surname at least five different ways.

The dispatch identified Mormon as a stage driver from Leadville and described Prindle as "a peaceable citizen and a stranger to Mormon." The Omaha Bee's Colorado column called him "a Darango desperado," while the Hartford Herald in Kentucky named him "Reed Moorman," son of the late John Moorman of Owensboro, raised in Breckenridge County. None of the papers stated his race or that of the men who hanged him.

According to the Republican's Durango special, Mormon and two companions entered a theater and gambling house early on the morning of the 10th. Drawing a revolver as he came in, he fired twice "with an oath," killing Prindle and wounding a young man in the arm. Condensed versions said he fired "without provocation" at men who were strangers to him. He fled but was overtaken and jailed.

That night vigilantes took Mormon from the jail and hanged him to a tree; a New Mexico version of the dispatch put the hour at 11 o'clock. The hanging took place "in the presence of several hundred citizens," and notice was given "that it would be death to the man who cut him down before morning." The papers did not say where in Durango the tree stood or name any of the vigilantes.

No report of an inquest, arrests or any action by county officials appears in the coverage. The Fremont County Record in Canon City noted only that he "was hung by vigilante" for killing "a perfect stranger to him," and the Omaha Bee said he was "promptly lynched by the citizens."

The Durango special went out from Denver and appeared on April 13 in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Cheyenne Daily Leader, the Memphis Public Ledger and the Las Vegas Morning Gazette. By April 14 it had reached the Savannah Morning News, the Portland Daily Press and the Chicago Daily Tribune, mostly verbatim. Weekly papers in Nevada, Colorado, Wisconsin, Missouri and Nebraska ran shorter digest paragraphs through the end of April.

Headlines cast the hanging as a deserved response to a killer: the Public Ledger's read "A Bully Walks into a Saloon and Kills a Man Without any Warning" over "Vigilants Take Care of Him," and Cheyenne's read "Prompt Action by Vigilates." Other dailies used plainer heads such as "A Murderer Lynched," "A Desperado Dealt With" and "A Colorado Lynching." On May 4 the Hartford Herald gave the story a local angle, remarking that "another Breckenridge boy has risen to distinction" by falling "from the drop of an impromptu gallows."

Accounts differed on several details, though nearly all trace to the same dispatch. The full special put the crowd at several hundred, while a condensed version gave one hundred. The special and the Colorado press placed the shooting and the hanging on the 10th, but a weekly news digest reprinted in Wisconsin said he was lynched "on the 13th inst." Most copies described the vigilantes as "unmasked," but the Savannah Morning News printed "some masked vigilantes."

bases: Vigilantes took a jailed man accused of murder from the Durango jail and hanged him to a tree before a crowd (A2, A5, A7).

Vigilantes, with no lawful authority, took Mormon from jail and hanged him for the accused killing of Polk Prindle (A2, A8); the group is described only as 'vigilantes', a 'mob' and 'the citizens', with no number given, so a group of three or more is inferred (A30, A34).

Every detailed account, including the Colorado and New Mexico versions, traces to one Denver Republican special from Durango (A2, A5, A20); the later briefs add no independent account of the hanging (A30, A34).

framing.detail: The Memphis Public Ledger headlined 'A Bully Walks into a Saloon and Kills a Man Without any Warning' and 'Vigilants Take Care of Him'; the Cheyenne Daily Leader ran 'Prompt Action by Vigilates'.
The Omaha Bee called him 'a Darango desperado' who was 'promptly lynched by the citizens'.
The Hartford Herald wrote sardonically that 'another Breckenridge boy has risen to distinction' by falling from 'an impromptu gallows'.
Most dailies ran the special verbatim under short heads such as 'A Murderer Lynched' and 'A Desperado Dealt With'.

conflicts.note: All describe one Leadville stage driver hanged at Durango; the variants are spellings in reprints, and only the Hartford Herald gives a different first name.

versions.value: night of the 10th, the day of the shooting

conflicts.note: The Durango special and the Colorado paper put both events on the 10th; the 13th appears only in a later weekly news digest and is likely the dispatch date. The Chicago Tribune's dateline reads 'April 18' (A11), apparently a misprint for 13.
The full special says several hundred; the condensed version says one hundred.
Most copies of the same special read 'unmasked'; the Savannah copy is likely a transcription change.
The Kentucky paper's phrase is a figure of speech in a sardonic paragraph; the special says a tree.
